prompt: What is a capital lease and what are the qualifications?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Lease Accounting
guidance: Must state that meeting ANY one criterion makes it a capital lease: ownership transfer/bargain purchase, lease term >75% of useful life, or PV of payments >90% of fair value.
explanation: A capital (finance) lease is economically an asset purchase financed by the lessor, and GAAP uses bright-line-ish tests to catch that substance. If a lease meets any one of the criteria it is capitalized: ownership transfers at the end or there's a bargain purchase option, the lease term covers more than about 75% of the asset's useful life, or the present value of lease payments exceeds about 90% of the asset's fair value. The logic behind each test is the same — if the lessee effectively consumes most of the asset's value or life, they're really buying it. Failing all criteria makes it an operating lease.

prompt: Why did GAAP historically use these bright-line thresholds, and what problem did they create that prompted the 2019 change?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should explain companies structured leases just under thresholds to keep them operating (off-balance-sheet), understating leverage, prompting ASC 842 to put all leases on the balance sheet.
explanation: The bright-line tests (like exactly 75% and 90%) gave companies a clear target to game: by structuring a lease to fall just short of every threshold, they could classify it as operating and keep both the asset and the debt off the balance sheet. This understated leverage and made the balance sheet look healthier than the economic reality. The 2019 standard (ASC 842) responded by requiring nearly all leases — operating and finance — to be recognized as a right-of-use asset and lease liability, restoring transparency while still preserving different expense patterns for the two types.

prompt: What is the accounting treatment for leases?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Lease Accounting
guidance: Must state that post-2019 both operating and capital leases record a ROU asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet, and mention the off-balance-sheet abuse motivation.
explanation: The major change effective 2019 (ASC 842) is that operating leases can no longer stay off the balance sheet. Both capital/finance and operating leases now require recognizing a right-of-use asset representing the right to use the leased asset and a corresponding lease liability for the obligation to pay. The reform was driven by companies deliberately structuring deals to qualify as operating leases and hide the associated financing. The income statement treatment still differs — finance leases split into interest and amortization while operating leases show a single lease expense — but the balance sheet now captures both.

prompt: A company with large operating lease commitments adopts ASC 842. What happens to its reported assets, liabilities, and leverage ratios, and how might this affect a leveraged buyout analysis?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should note gross-up of balance sheet (ROU asset and lease liability rise), reported leverage increases, and PE analysts may treat lease liabilities as debt-like when assessing capital structure and coverage.
explanation: Adopting ASC 842 grosses up the balance sheet: a right-of-use asset appears on the asset side and a matching lease liability on the liability side, so both totals rise materially for lease-heavy businesses. Reported leverage optically increases because the lease liability now shows as an obligation. In an LBO context this matters because analysts must decide whether to treat lease liabilities as debt when computing enterprise value, net debt, and coverage ratios — capitalized leases are increasingly viewed as debt-like fixed obligations. Mishandling them can distort purchase price, credit capacity, and comparability across targets that lease versus own.

prompt: You're considering a potential investment in a desk manufacturer. What do COGS and SG&A consist of?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must correctly split direct production costs (raw materials, direct labor, production-related depreciation) into COGS and indirect/operating costs (marketing, sales, distribution, admin, HQ) into SG&A.
explanation: The dividing line is whether a cost is directly tied to producing the product. COGS captures direct production inputs: raw materials like wood and hardware, the wages of the workers actually building the desks, and depreciation of the factory and production equipment. SG&A captures the costs of running the business that aren't part of making the product — advertising, sales commissions, distribution, and administrative overhead like headquarters rent and executive pay. Getting this split right matters because it drives gross margin (revenue minus COGS) versus operating margin.

prompt: If the desk manufacturer decided to reclassify its production supervisors' salaries from COGS to SG&A, what happens to gross margin, operating margin, and EBITDA, and why might this be misleading?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should note gross margin rises (COGS falls), operating margin/EBITDA unchanged, and warn that reclassification inflates gross margin optically without changing economics, hurting comparability.
explanation: Moving a cost from COGS to SG&A lowers COGS, so gross margin rises even though nothing about the actual economics changed. Operating income and EBITDA are unaffected because the same dollars are still expensed above the EBIT line — only the classification within operating costs shifted. This is misleading because gross margin is a key comparability metric across peers, and reclassifying production costs can make the company look more efficient at manufacturing than it really is. An analyst should normalize cost classifications before comparing margins across companies.

prompt: When and why would you capitalize vs. expense a purchase?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Answer must tie the decision to the period over which benefits accrue: costs with multi-year benefit are capitalized (put on the balance sheet and depreciated/amortized), single-period costs are expensed immediately. Should reference the matching principle.
explanation: The core intuition is the matching principle: you want expenses to line up in time with the revenue they help generate. If a purchase only helps this year (rent, salaries, supplies), you expense it now. If it delivers value over many years (a factory, equipment, sometimes R&D), you capitalize it, meaning you park the cost on the balance sheet as an asset and gradually run it through the income statement via depreciation or amortization. Capitalizing smooths the hit to earnings and better reflects the economic reality that the benefit is spread over time. The tradeoff is that capitalizing keeps near-term earnings higher but requires judgment on useful life.

prompt: A company suddenly starts capitalizing costs it used to expense (say software development). What happens to its earnings, cash flow, and balance sheet in the near term, and why might an analyst be skeptical?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should note EBIT/net income rise (expense removed from IS), operating cash flow rises while investing cash flow falls (net cash unchanged), assets grow, and flag the earnings-quality/aggressive-accounting red flag.
explanation: Shifting a cost from expensed to capitalized removes it from the income statement in the current period, so operating expenses drop and reported earnings and EBIT rise. On the cash flow statement the cash outflow moves from operating activities to investing activities (capex), which inflates operating cash flow even though total cash is unchanged. The balance sheet shows a larger asset base that will depreciate over future years. Analysts get suspicious because capitalization is a common earnings-management lever: it boosts current profits and operating cash flow while pushing the expense into the future, so a policy change unaccompanied by a real change in the business is an earnings-quality red flag.

prompt: How is a Deferred Tax Asset created? A Deferred Tax Liability?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must correctly define DTL (book taxes > cash taxes, future obligation to pay more) and DTA (book taxes < cash taxes, future benefit of paying less), driven by temporary timing differences.
explanation: Deferred taxes exist because the tax return and the financial statements recognize income and expenses on different schedules, creating temporary timing differences. A Deferred Tax Liability arises when the company reports higher tax expense on its books than it actually pays in cash today; the shortfall is a future obligation, so it sits on the balance sheet as a liability. A Deferred Tax Asset is the mirror image: the company pays more cash tax now than its book expense implies, so it has effectively prepaid taxes and will owe less later, a future benefit recorded as an asset. The clean test is to ask whether the timing difference means you'll pay more tax later (DTL) or less tax later (DTA).

prompt: A company has $200m of net operating loss carryforwards. How does that create a DTA, and what could force the company to write it down?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should explain NOLs shelter future taxable income creating a DTA (NOL times tax rate), and that a valuation allowance is required if it becomes more-likely-than-not the company won't generate enough future income to use them.
explanation: Net operating loss carryforwards let a company offset future taxable income, so they represent a future reduction in cash taxes, which is exactly what a DTA captures; the asset equals the usable NOL multiplied by the expected tax rate. The catch is that the DTA only has value if the firm actually earns enough future profit to absorb the losses. Under the more-likely-than-not standard, if management concludes the company probably won't generate sufficient taxable income, it must record a valuation allowance that reduces the DTA, hitting the income statement. This is why struggling companies often carry large valuation allowances against their NOL-driven DTAs.

prompt: Explain the difference between book and tax depreciation?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must explain that companies use straight-line for books and accelerated for taxes, that this defers cash taxes in early years, and that the resulting timing difference creates a DTL that reverses over time.
explanation: Companies keep two sets of depreciation schedules for the same asset because their goals differ: financial reporting wants smooth, representative earnings, while tax reporting wants to minimize cash taxes as early as possible. So they typically use straight-line depreciation on the books and an accelerated method (like MACRS) on the tax return. Accelerated depreciation front-loads the deduction, so in early years the tax return shows a bigger expense, lower taxable income, and lower cash taxes than the books imply. That gap between book tax expense and cash tax paid creates a Deferred Tax Liability. Over the asset's life total depreciation is identical under both methods, so the DTL builds up early and reverses in later years.

prompt: Walk through what happens to the DTL over the full life of an asset depreciated straight-line for books and accelerated for tax. When does it peak and when is it zero?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should show DTL grows in early years when tax depreciation exceeds book, peaks around the crossover, then reverses as book depreciation exceeds tax, netting to zero at end of life since total depreciation is equal.
explanation: Because both methods depreciate the same total cost, the difference is purely timing. In the early years accelerated tax depreciation exceeds straight-line book depreciation, so cash taxes are lower than book taxes and the DTL grows. The DTL reaches its maximum around the point where the two depreciation schedules cross. In later years the relationship flips: book depreciation now exceeds the smaller remaining tax depreciation, cash taxes exceed book taxes, and the DTL unwinds. By the end of the asset's useful life cumulative depreciation is identical under both methods, so the DTL nets back to zero.

prompt: Why do DTAs and DTLs get created in M&A deals?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must explain that PPA writes up assets on the GAAP balance sheet but a stock deal keeps the tax basis unchanged, so incremental book D&A isn't tax deductible, creating a DTL.
explanation: In an acquisition, purchase accounting requires the acquirer to mark the target's assets to fair value on the GAAP balance sheet, often writing them up. But in a stock deal the tax basis of those assets carries over unchanged, so the tax return sees no write-up. That means the extra depreciation and amortization generated by the write-up shows up as an expense on the books but is not deductible for tax purposes. As a result book taxes look lower than the cash taxes the company must actually pay, and that future obligation to pay taxes on income the books don't fully show is recorded as a Deferred Tax Liability. The reverse (a write-down or acquired NOLs) can instead create a DTA.

prompt: Why does a stock deal typically create a DTL from asset write-ups while an asset deal (or 338(h)(10) election) usually does not?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should explain that in an asset deal the tax basis is stepped up to match fair value so the write-up IS tax deductible, eliminating the book-tax difference and the DTL, whereas a stock deal leaves tax basis unchanged.
explanation: The whole reason the DTL appears is that in a stock deal the GAAP asset values step up but the tax basis stays at the target's historical carryover level, so the incremental D&A is non-deductible. In an asset deal, or a stock deal with a 338(h)(10) election, the transaction is treated as a purchase of assets for tax purposes, so the tax basis also steps up to fair value. Now the write-up is depreciable and amortizable for tax too, book and tax D&A align, and there's no timing difference to record. This is precisely why buyers value the tax shield from a stepped-up basis and why sellers often demand a higher price to compensate for the extra tax an asset deal triggers for them.

prompt: What happens to the financial statements when there is a $100 write-down of an asset?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must walk all three statements: IS pre-tax loss of $100 and after-tax $80 at 20% tax; CFS add back the $100 non-cash charge so cash rises $20; BS assets down $80 net, retained earnings down $80, balances.
explanation: Start on the income statement: a $100 write-down is a pre-tax loss, and at a 20% tax rate the tax shield saves $20, so net income falls by $80. On the cash flow statement, begin with net income down $80, then add back the full $100 write-down because it's a non-cash charge, netting to a $20 increase in cash. That $20 is real cash saved on taxes. On the balance sheet, the written-down asset drops $100 but cash rises $20, so total assets fall $80; on the other side retained earnings falls $80 from the lower net income, and the balance sheet stays balanced.

prompt: Now suppose instead of a write-down the company records a $100 goodwill impairment that is NOT tax deductible. How do the three statements change versus the deductible write-down?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should recognize no tax shield: pre-tax loss $100, after-tax loss also $100 (no deduction), CFS add-back $100 nets cash change to zero, assets down $100, retained earnings down $100.
explanation: The key difference is that if the impairment is not tax deductible, there is no tax benefit, so the pre-tax loss of $100 flows straight through as a $100 reduction in net income. On the cash flow statement net income is down $100 but you add back the full $100 non-cash impairment, so the net change in cash is exactly zero, unlike the deductible case where cash rose by the tax shield. On the balance sheet the asset (goodwill) falls $100 with no offsetting cash increase, so total assets drop $100, and retained earnings falls $100, keeping it balanced. This is why the tax treatment of a charge matters: a non-deductible impairment provides no cash benefit.

prompt: How does a $100 equity bailout[16] of a company flow through the financial statements?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must show no income statement impact, CFS +$100 in financing activities, BS cash up $100 and shareholders' equity up $100. Bonus for noting a bailout is essentially cheap primary equity from the government.
explanation: An equity bailout is just the government buying newly issued primary shares from the company, so treat it like any equity raise. Issuing stock is not revenue or an expense, so the income statement is untouched. On the cash flow statement it's a financing inflow of $100, and with nothing else moving, cash rises $100. On the balance sheet, cash goes up $100 on the asset side and shareholders' equity (common stock/APIC) goes up $100 on the other side, so it balances. The only special flavor of a bailout is the motive: the government accepts a below-market return, effectively supplying capital at a lower cost than the market would.

prompt: Contrast the three-statement impact of a $100 equity bailout with a $100 government loan (debt). How do the statements and future income statements differ?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Should note both raise cash $100 via financing, but equity adds to shareholders' equity with no IS impact, while debt adds a $100 liability and creates future interest expense that reduces net income (with a tax shield).
explanation: Both a bailout equity injection and a loan bring in $100 of cash through financing activities, so day one the cash flow statement and cash balance look identical. The difference is on the other side of the balance sheet and in future periods. Equity adds $100 to shareholders' equity and carries no contractual repayment or interest, so the income statement stays clean going forward. Debt instead books a $100 liability, and in subsequent periods generates interest expense that lowers pre-tax income, partially offset by a tax shield, and eventually must be repaid. So debt is cheaper if the firm survives but riskier and drags future earnings, while equity dilutes ownership but adds no fixed burden.

prompt: What are trading securities? How do they differ from Held to Maturity and Available for Sale?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must classify all three by holding intent and correctly place valuation (fair value vs amortized cost) and where unrealized gains/losses flow (IS vs AOCI vs none).
explanation: The key is management's intent, which drives both how the security is valued and where the mark-to-market changes go. Trading securities are meant to be flipped soon, so they sit at fair value and their unrealized gains/losses hit the income statement immediately, making earnings volatile. Available-for-sale sits in the middle: it's also carried at fair value, but the unrealized swings park in AOCI (equity) and only reach the income statement when actually sold. Held-to-maturity means the company plans and is able to hold the bond until it matures, so day-to-day price moves are irrelevant and it's carried at amortized cost. Think of it as a spectrum from most active (trading, IS impact) to most passive (HTM, cost basis).

prompt: A company holds an available-for-sale bond that has dropped in value, and management now believes the loss is permanent (other-than-temporary impairment). How does the accounting treatment change versus a normal temporary decline?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must explain that a temporary AFS decline sits in AOCI, but an OTTI/credit loss is recognized through the income statement, reducing net income.
explanation: Normally an AFS unrealized loss just accumulates in AOCI and never touches earnings until sale. But when the decline is judged other-than-temporary (a credit loss under current CECL/impairment rules), that portion is reclassified out of AOCI and run through the income statement as a realized loss. This prevents companies from indefinitely hiding real economic losses in equity. The distinction matters because it converts a balance-sheet-only event into an earnings hit, which is why the impairment judgment is scrutinized.

prompt: What would be the impact on the financial statements of switching from capitalizing R&D to expensing it immediately or vice versa?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must explain capitalizing shifts cost from IS expense to a depreciating asset, raising near-term net income, but note the Year 1 cash impact via the lost tax shield.
explanation: Expensing R&D immediately hits the income statement in full, lowering net income now; capitalizing instead books an asset and spreads the cost via amortization over several years, so near-term net income is higher. The counterintuitive part is cash: capitalizing actually leaves you with less cash in Year 1 because you record a smaller expense, get a smaller tax deduction, and therefore pay more tax that year. The cash outflow for the R&D itself still happens either way, but it moves to investing activities when capitalized. So capitalizing = higher earnings, lower Year 1 cash flow by the amount of the lost tax shield; expensing = the reverse.

prompt: Under U.S. tax law changes, R&D must now be capitalized and amortized for tax purposes over five years even if expensed for book purposes. Walk through how this creates a deferred tax asset and its cash impact.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must show that book expense exceeds tax deduction in early years, raising taxable income and current taxes paid, and creating a DTA that reverses later.
explanation: When you expense R&D on the books but the tax code forces you to amortize it, your taxable income in early years is higher than your book pretax income, so you pay more cash tax up front. That timing difference creates a deferred tax asset, because you've effectively prepaid tax that will reverse as the amortization deductions come through in later years. The near-term effect is a real cash drain even though book earnings are unchanged. This is a good example of how book and tax treatment can diverge and why cash taxes, not the effective tax rate, matter for valuation.

prompt: A company sells an asset for cash at a $300mm gain. How does this affect the financial statements?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must walk all three statements: after-tax gain to NI, add-back/reclass on CFS with full proceeds in CFI, and BS balancing via cash up, PP&E down, retained earnings up.
explanation: A gain on sale is a non-operating item that flows through the income statement pre-tax, so at a 20% tax rate the $300mm gain becomes $240mm of net income. On the cash flow statement, that $240mm lifts net income in operating activities, but the $300mm gain is a non-cash accounting item relative to operations, so the full cash proceeds show up in investing while the gain gets reconciled out. The balance sheet balances because cash rises by the proceeds, PP&E falls by the asset's book value, and retained earnings rises by the $240mm after-tax gain. The trick candidates miss is that only the gain, not the whole proceeds, is taxed and hits earnings.

prompt: Now assume the same asset had a book value of $500mm and was sold for $200mm cash (a loss), with a 25% tax rate. Walk through all three statements.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must compute the $300mm pretax loss, a $75mm tax benefit, $225mm net loss to NI, $200mm cash into CFI, PP&E down $500mm, and confirm the balance sheet ties.
explanation: Here the asset's book value is $500mm but you only get $200mm, so there's a $300mm pretax loss that reduces net income; at 25% the tax benefit is $75mm, leaving a $225mm after-tax loss. On cash flow, net income falls $225mm in operations but the $300mm loss is a non-cash add-back, and the $200mm of actual proceeds lands in investing. The balance sheet ties because assets change by +$200mm cash minus $500mm PP&E (net -$300mm), matched on the equity side by retained earnings falling $225mm and the $75mm tax benefit reducing taxes payable/cash tax. The lesson is that a loss produces a tax shield rather than a tax cost, flipping the sign of the tax line.

prompt: Following on from "A company sells an asset for cash at a $300mm gain. How does this affect the financial statements?" — What is the difference between the two questions above ($300 gain on sale and selling a pair of jeans for $20 that cost $10)?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must distinguish that inventory sales run through revenue and COGS (operating), while non-inventory asset sales produce a below-EBIT gain/loss.
explanation: The distinction is about what kind of asset is being sold and therefore where it lands on the income statement. Selling inventory is the company's ordinary business, so it books revenue and the matching cost of goods sold, and the margin sits within operating income above EBIT. Selling a long-term asset like a piece of equipment or a building is not the core business, so instead of gross revenue you only record the gain or loss versus book value, and that line sits below EBIT as a non-operating item. In short: inventory affects revenue and COGS; other assets affect only a gain/loss line.

prompt: Why does it matter to an analyst whether a $50mm boost to earnings came from a gain on asset sale versus from core product sales, even though both increase net income by the same amount?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must address quality/recurrence of earnings: gains are one-time and non-operating, so they inflate NI but shouldn't be capitalized into a multiple; core sales are recurring.
explanation: Both increase net income equally, but an analyst cares about the quality and repeatability of earnings. A gain on an asset sale is a one-time, non-operating event that won't recur next year, so it shouldn't be valued at the same multiple as recurring operating profit. Product sales reflect the ongoing earning power of the business, which is what drives valuation. That's why analysts strip out gains and losses to get to a normalized, operating figure like EBIT or adjusted EBITDA before applying a multiple.

prompt: A company purchases $10mm of Inventory from suppliers on credit. What is the impact on the financial statements?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state no IS impact until sold, CFS offset of inventory increase by AP increase (no net cash), and BS asset/liability both up $10mm.
explanation: Buying inventory on credit is purely a balance sheet and non-cash event at the moment of purchase. There's no income statement effect because expense is only recognized as COGS when the inventory is actually sold, matching cost with revenue. On the cash flow statement, the $10mm build in inventory (a use of cash) is exactly offset by the $10mm increase in accounts payable (a source of cash), so net cash is unchanged, which makes sense because no cash has left the company. The balance sheet stays balanced with inventory up $10mm on the asset side and accounts payable up $10mm on the liability side.

prompt: Continue the scenario: the company later sells all $10mm of that inventory for $16mm cash, and separately pays down the $10mm accounts payable. Walk through the combined financial statement impact.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must show $16mm revenue less $10mm COGS = $6mm gross profit taxed, NI up by after-tax amount, inventory to zero, AP paid reducing cash, and the BS tying.
explanation: When the inventory sells, you recognize $16mm revenue and $10mm COGS, producing $6mm of pretax profit; after tax (say 25%) net income rises about $4.5mm. On cash flow, inventory falls $10mm (a source of cash) and cash comes in from the sale, while paying down the $10mm payable is a $10mm use of cash. Net cash rises by the sale proceeds minus the payable repayment and taxes. The balance sheet ties because inventory goes to zero, AP goes to zero, cash reflects the net movement, and retained earnings absorbs the after-tax profit. This ties the earlier non-cash purchase to its eventual earnings and cash realization.

prompt: What is the allowance method? What is the direct method? What are the benefits / drawbacks to each?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must define both methods (provision via contra-AR vs recognize at default), and note allowance is more conservative and matches better but relies on estimates/is more manipulable.
explanation: Both methods deal with receivables you don't expect to collect, but they differ in timing. The allowance method estimates future bad debts up front, recording an expense now and a contra-asset (allowance for doubtful accounts) that reduces net AR, so it recognizes the cost in the same period as the related revenue. The direct write-off method waits until a specific account is actually deemed uncollectible before recording any expense. The allowance method is required under GAAP because it respects the matching principle and is more conservative, but it depends on management estimates, which adds complexity and creates room for manipulation. The direct method is simpler and objective but distorts matching by recognizing the loss too late.

prompt: A company increases its allowance for doubtful accounts by $5mm this period. Walk through the impact on all three financial statements.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must show a $5mm bad debt expense reducing pretax income (after-tax NI hit), non-cash add-back on CFS with no cash change beyond the tax effect, and net AR reduced via the contra account on the BS.
explanation: Boosting the allowance by $5mm records a $5mm bad debt expense on the income statement, cutting pretax income and, after a tax shield, net income by the after-tax amount. On the cash flow statement, that expense is non-cash, so you add it back in operations; the only real cash effect is lower taxes, so operating cash actually improves slightly relative to the earnings hit. On the balance sheet, the allowance is a contra-asset that reduces net accounts receivable by $5mm, and retained earnings falls by the after-tax loss, keeping it balanced. This shows how a purely estimated provision moves earnings without any customer actually defaulting yet.

prompt: You sell a shirt which costs you $10 for $20 dollars on credit. What is the impact on the financial statements?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must walk through IS (revenue $20, COGS $10, net income +$8 at 20% tax), CFS (add back inventory decrease $10, subtract AR increase $20, net cash -$2), and BS balancing (assets +$8, equity +$8).
explanation: The trick here is that selling on credit means no cash actually arrives, so you have to think in accruals versus cash. On the income statement you book $20 revenue and $10 COGS, giving $10 pretax profit and $8 net income after a 20% tax. On the cash flow statement you start from that $8, then add back the $10 of inventory you shipped out (a source of cash) and subtract the $20 rise in accounts receivable (a use of cash), so cash actually falls $2. The balance sheet balances because assets rise $8 (cash -$2, AR +$20, inventory -$10) and equity rises $8 from retained earnings. The counterintuitive lesson is that a profitable sale can drain cash when it's on credit and taxes are paid in cash.

prompt: Same shirt sale for $20 on credit costing $10, but now the customer prepaid you $20 in cash last quarter and you're recognizing the revenue now. What's the impact on the three statements this period?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must recognize deferred revenue is drawn down (liability -$20), no AR is created, net income +$8, and cash actually rises because the prior cash inflow is now matched with only $10 inventory outflow and $2 tax.
explanation: When cash was collected in advance it sat as a deferred revenue liability, so recognizing revenue now doesn't create a receivable. Net income still rises $8 (revenue $20, COGS $10, tax $2). On the CFS you add back the $10 inventory reduction, but you also reduce deferred revenue by $20 as a use of cash offsetting the earlier inflow, so this period cash changes by only -$2 (the tax paid), similar mechanics but no AR. The balance sheet shows inventory -$10, deferred revenue liability -$20, retained earnings +$8, and cash -$2, which balances. The point is timing: prepayment shifts the cash inflow to an earlier period.

prompt: You own a hamburger business. What is the combined impact on the financial statements of buying a hot dog on credit for $3 and selling the hot dog to a person on credit for $8?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must net two credit transactions: operating profit +$5, net income +$4, CFS impact of AP +$3 and AR +$8 giving net cash -$1, and balance sheet balancing.
explanation: This is the same credit-sale logic but with both purchase and sale on credit, so you track two working capital items. Operating profit is $8 revenue minus $3 cost equals $5, and net income is $4 after 20% tax. On the CFS, start from $4, add the $3 increase in accounts payable (you haven't paid the supplier, a source of cash) and subtract the $8 increase in AR (you haven't collected, a use of cash), giving net cash of -$1, which equals the tax you actually paid. The balance sheet balances: assets rise $7 (cash -$1, AR +$8), while liabilities and equity rise $7 (AP +$3, retained earnings +$4). The insight is that even with nothing paid or received in cash, taxes are cash and drag you negative.

prompt: You buy the hot dog for $3 cash but sell it on credit for $8. How does the cash flow impact differ from the all-credit version, and why does the tax payment still matter?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must show net income still +$4, but now no AP increase and a $3 cash outflow for inventory purchase plus $8 AR, so net cash falls by more (-$4), and note taxes remain a cash item.
explanation: Paying cash for the hot dog removes the accounts payable cushion, so you lose the $3 source of cash. Net income is unchanged at $4 because the income statement doesn't care whether the purchase was cash or credit. On the CFS you start from $4, add nothing back for AP, subtract $8 for the AR increase, and the $3 cash purchase already reduced cash, netting to roughly -$4 depending on how inventory flows. The lesson is that financing terms change cash timing dramatically even when reported profit is identical.

prompt: Two companies have the same Profit margins but different EBITDA margins. What could be some possible causes?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must identify the line items between EBITDA and net income (D&A, net interest, taxes, non-recurring items) and give a plausible cause for at least three that would offset to equalize net margin.
explanation: EBITDA and net income differ only by depreciation and amortization, net interest expense, taxes, and sometimes non-recurring items, so if net margins are equal but EBITDA margins differ, one of those bridge items must be absorbing the difference. A company with a higher EBITDA margin might carry more debt or a higher cost of debt, so heavier interest expense pulls it back down to the same net margin. Alternatively it could be more capital-intensive with higher D&A, sit in a higher tax jurisdiction, or have taken losses on non-core asset sales below the EBITDA line. The disciplined way to answer is to name the bridge and then attach a business reason to each item. This tests whether you actually understand what EBITDA excludes.

prompt: Two companies have identical EBITDA margins but very different free cash flow margins. What could explain that?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must move below EBITDA into capex, cash taxes, cash interest, and working capital changes, distinguishing accrual EBITDA from actual cash generation.
explanation: EBITDA ignores everything that turns operating profit into real cash, so equal EBITDA can hide big cash differences. One company might have far higher maintenance or growth capex, heavier cash interest from more debt, higher cash taxes, or a working capital profile that consumes cash as it grows. A high-EBITDA but capital-hungry business can convert far less to free cash flow than a capital-light peer. This is exactly why PE investors care about FCF conversion, not just EBITDA.

prompt: If you had to decide whether or not to invest in a company based on a single financial statement, which would you pick? What if you could pick two?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must pick the cash flow statement with a cash-generation/IRR rationale, and for two statements add the balance sheet, noting it enables leverage/solvency analysis and connects the other statements.
explanation: If you can only see one statement, the cash flow statement wins because investment returns ultimately come from cash, not accrual earnings, and it strips out accounting choices to show what the business actually generates and consumes. For a distressed company the balance sheet may be more revealing because it shows liquidation value and solvency. Given two statements, most would pair the CFS with the balance sheet, since together they let you assess cash generation, leverage, liquidity, and asset backing, and multiple periods of balance sheets even imply cash flows. The reasoning matters more than the exact pick, so long as it's grounded in cash and value.

prompt: Why might the income statement alone be dangerously misleading for judging a company, even a profitable one?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must explain accrual accounting lets reported profit diverge from cash, and cite examples like aggressive revenue recognition, non-cash gains, or growing companies burning cash despite reported earnings.
explanation: The income statement is built on accruals, so a company can report strong profits while bleeding cash or while relying on non-cash gains and aggressive revenue recognition. It says nothing directly about how much debt sits on the balance sheet, how much capex is required, or how working capital is trending. A fast-growing firm can show rising net income while its cash balance collapses because receivables and inventory absorb cash faster than profits arrive. That gap between earnings and cash is precisely where accounting manipulation and business fragility hide.

prompt: How can earnings be manipulated through accounting procedures?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must list several distinct levers: inventory method (FIFO/LIFO), depreciation schedules, revenue recognition timing, capitalizing vs expensing, asset writedowns/valuation estimates, and timing of non-recurring items.
explanation: Earnings quality questions test whether you know where management has discretion. Big levers include inventory costing (LIFO vs FIFO changes COGS and thus earnings in inflationary times), depreciation and amortization schedules that shift expense across periods, and revenue recognition timing where looser standards pull revenue forward, often flagged by ballooning receivables. Management can also capitalize costs like R&D or interest to boost near-term earnings, time asset writedowns and non-recurring items, and lean on subjective valuations for mark-to-model or hard-to-value assets. The unifying theme is that anywhere estimates or timing choices exist, reported earnings can be nudged, so analysts cross-check against cash flow.

prompt: A company's net income is growing steadily but its cash flow from operations is flat or declining. What red flags would you investigate?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must connect the earnings-cash divergence to specific suspects: rising DSO/receivables, inventory buildup, capitalized costs, one-time gains inflating income, or aggressive revenue recognition.
explanation: A persistent gap where earnings rise but operating cash doesn't is the classic signature of low earnings quality. You'd examine whether receivables are growing faster than sales (channel stuffing or loosened credit terms), whether inventory is piling up, and whether costs are being capitalized rather than expensed. You'd also check for non-cash or one-time gains propping up net income. The tool here is the accruals ratio: a widening spread between accrual earnings and cash generation is a warning that reported profits may not be sustainable or real.

prompt: Could a company have negative shareholders' equity? What would this imply?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must confirm negative equity is possible and give causes: accumulated losses eroding retained earnings, and dividends/recaps exceeding equity, plus note it doesn't automatically mean insolvency.
explanation: Yes, shareholders' equity can go negative because it's a residual accounting figure, not a market value. Sustained net losses drain retained earnings until accumulated deficits exceed paid-in capital, or a company can deliberately pay out a dividend larger than its equity, which is common in a leveraged dividend recapitalization where a sponsor loads on debt and pulls cash out. Negative book equity signals that liabilities exceed the accounting value of assets, but it doesn't necessarily mean the company is insolvent or unable to operate, especially if it generates strong cash flow. Many healthy, heavily-leveraged buyout companies run with negative book equity precisely because of large debt-funded distributions.

prompt: In a dividend recapitalization that pushes book equity negative, what should an investor look at instead of book equity to judge whether the company is actually healthy?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must pivot from book equity to cash flow coverage, leverage ratios (debt/EBITDA), interest coverage, and enterprise/market value versus debt.
explanation: Book equity becomes meaningless in a recap because it's been intentionally distributed out, so you judge health by the company's ability to service and repay debt. You look at leverage measured as net debt to EBITDA, interest coverage ratios, and free cash flow relative to required debt payments. You also compare enterprise value or a market valuation of the equity against the debt load to see if there's real cushion. The point is that solvency and creditworthiness are about cash generation and debt capacity, not the accounting residual on the balance sheet.

prompt: How would a dividend recap impact the 3 statements in an LBO?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state the income statement is unchanged, that financing cash flow nets to roughly zero (debt in, dividend out), and that on the balance sheet liabilities rise while equity falls via retained earnings.
explanation: A dividend recap is when a company raises new debt purely to pay a dividend to its equity owners rather than to fund operations or growth. Because no operations change and issuing debt/paying a dividend are financing and balance-sheet events, the income statement is untouched at the moment of the recap (interest expense only shows up in future periods). On the cash flow statement, cash from financing gets a boost from the new debt drawdown and an offsetting reduction from the dividend paid out, so net cash is roughly flat if you ignore fees. On the balance sheet, liabilities increase by the new debt and shareholders' equity falls by the same amount as the dividend reduces retained earnings, so total assets are basically unchanged.

prompt: One year after a dividend recap, how do the three statements look compared to a scenario where the recap never happened?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Answer must recognize new interest expense flows through the income statement (reducing net income and taxes), and trace the resulting effects on cash flow and the debt/equity balances.
explanation: Once a full year passes, the added debt now carries interest expense, so the income statement shows lower pre-tax income, a tax shield from the deductible interest, and therefore lower net income. On the cash flow statement, lower net income reduces operating cash flow, though the tax savings partially cushion it; principal is only affected if there's mandatory amortization. On the balance sheet, retained earnings grow more slowly because net income is smaller, and cash is lower than the no-recap case, so the leverage taken on genuinely reduces the equity value being built over time — which is exactly why sponsors weigh the yield to LPs against the drag on future returns.

prompt: Compared to the prior fiscal year, a company's average selling price increased by 10%, while the number of customers decreased by 10%. What was the effect on revenue?
source_ref: Priced In — Accounting Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must multiply the two factors (1.10 x 0.90 = 0.99) and conclude revenue fell ~1%, not that they cancel out.
explanation: The instinct is that a 10% price increase and a 10% volume decrease cancel to zero, but percentage changes compound multiplicatively rather than add. Revenue is price times volume, so you multiply 1.10 by 0.90, which gives 0.99. That means revenue actually declined by 1%. The asymmetry exists because the 10% price gain is applied to the original base while the 10% volume drop shrinks that base first — equal-sized offsetting percentage moves always net to a small loss.

prompt: A company grew volume 20% and cut price 20%; the CEO says revenue is flat. Is he right, and what price change would exactly offset a 20% volume gain to keep revenue flat?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Accounting Refresher
guidance: Must show 1.20 x 0.80 = 0.96 (a 4% decline), and derive that offsetting a 20% volume gain requires a price factor of 1/1.20, i.e. an ~16.7% price cut.
explanation: The CEO is wrong: 1.20 times 0.80 equals 0.96, so revenue actually falls 4%. To keep revenue exactly flat while volume rises 20%, the price factor must be the reciprocal, 1/1.20 ≈ 0.833, meaning price can only fall about 16.7%, not 20%. This reinforces that percentage moves compound, and the offsetting move is always smaller in magnitude than the gain it's cancelling.

prompt: What's the difference between a bond and a loan?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must distinguish along liquidity/secondary-market tradability and origination/ownership (bank-originated loans vs. issuer-issued bonds), noting bonds carry public reporting.
explanation: Both are debt, but the practical distinctions come down to how they trade and how they originate. Loans are typically private bilateral or syndicated agreements originated by banks, with thin secondary liquidity and privately-held marks, while bonds are securities issued directly by the borrower that trade actively in public secondary markets at premium, par, or discount. Because bonds are public securities they usually come with more stringent disclosure and reporting requirements. The line has blurred with loan syndication and securitization, but the origination source and tradability remain the core differences.

prompt: In an LBO capital structure, why is a term loan typically floating-rate and senior secured while high-yield bonds are often fixed-rate and unsecured, and how does that affect their relative pricing?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Must connect seniority/security and rate structure to risk: loans sit higher in the waterfall with collateral (lower spread, floating over a reference rate), bonds are subordinated/unsecured (higher fixed coupon), reflecting risk and investor base.
explanation: Term loans in an LBO are usually senior secured and rank first in the payment waterfall with a lien on assets, so lenders bear less loss-given-default risk and accept a lower spread, quoted as a floating rate over a benchmark like SOFR. High-yield bonds typically sit below the loans, unsecured and subordinated, so investors demand a higher fixed coupon to compensate for greater downside. The floating-vs-fixed split also reflects investor bases — bank/CLO loan buyers prefer floating exposure, while bond investors want locked-in fixed yields. The result is that the loan tranche prices tighter and the bond tranche prices wider, matching each instrument's position in the risk hierarchy.

prompt: How do you value a bond?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state bonds are valued by discounting expected coupon and principal cash flows at a risk-appropriate rate, and note debt investors focus on downside/coverage given capped upside.
explanation: A bond is valued the same way as any asset: project its future cash flows — the periodic coupons plus the return of face value at maturity — and discount them back at a rate that reflects the security's riskiness. The higher the perceived credit risk, the higher the discount rate and the lower the price. What separates debt from equity analysis is that a bondholder's upside is capped at getting paid coupons and par, so the analytical energy goes into downside protection, default probability, and coverage/capacity rather than growth optionality.

prompt: A bond has a 5% coupon and trades at a price of 92. Is its yield to maturity above or below 5%, and explain the relationship between coupon, price, and yield.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Must state YTM is above 5% because the bond trades at a discount, and explain the inverse relationship: price below par implies yield above coupon.
explanation: When a bond trades below par (a price of 92 versus 100), its yield to maturity is higher than its coupon rate, so above 5%. The intuition is that a buyer paying only 92 still collects the full 5% coupon on face plus a gain of 8 at maturity, boosting the effective return. Price and yield move inversely: as required yield rises above the coupon, the price must fall below par to make the fixed cash flows competitive, and vice versa for a premium bond.

prompt: Which corporate bond would have a higher coupon, a AAA or a BBB?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must say the BBB bond has the higher coupon because it is lower-rated and carries greater default risk, requiring more yield compensation.
explanation: Credit ratings rank default risk, with AAA being the safest and BBB sitting near the bottom of investment grade. Investors demand extra yield for taking on more risk, so a lower-rated BBB issuer must offer a higher coupon than a pristine AAA issuer to attract buyers. That incremental yield over a comparable risk-free benchmark is the credit spread, and it widens as ratings fall. So the BBB bond pays the higher coupon.

prompt: During a recession, why do credit spreads on BBB bonds widen more than spreads on AAA bonds, and what does that imply about their relative price declines?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Must explain that lower-rated credits have higher default sensitivity to the cycle, so their spreads widen disproportionately, causing larger price drops (higher spread duration/credit risk).
explanation: In a downturn, the probability of default rises across the board, but it rises far more for weaker, lower-rated issuers whose cash flows have less cushion. Investors respond by demanding much wider spreads on BBB paper than on AAA paper, whose default risk stays negligible. Because a bond's price falls as its required yield rises, the larger spread widening on BBB bonds produces a larger price decline. This is why lower-rated credit behaves more like equity in stressed markets, exhibiting greater cyclicality and drawdown.

prompt: What is the duration of a bond? What is convexity?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must define duration as weighted-average time to receive cash flows / price sensitivity to rates (~x% price move per 1% rate move), and convexity as the positive curvature of the price-yield relationship (second derivative positive).
explanation: Duration measures how sensitive a bond's price is to interest rate changes: a duration of 5 means a 1% rise in rates drops the price by roughly 5%, and it can also be read as the weighted-average time until you recoup your investment through cash flows. But that linear approximation isn't exact — the true price-yield relationship curves. Convexity captures this curvature: because the second derivative of price with respect to yield is positive, prices rise more when rates fall than they drop when rates rise by the same amount. This convexity is beneficial to bondholders and grows with maturity, which is why sensitivity differences widen as you extend out the curve.

prompt: Two bonds have the same duration of 6, but one is a zero-coupon bond and the other pays a high coupon. Which has greater convexity, and why does convexity matter more in a volatile rate environment?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Must state the zero-coupon bond (cash flows concentrated at one distant point) has less convexity than a same-duration coupon bond whose cash flows are more dispersed; and note convexity is valuable because it improves outcomes under large rate swings in either direction.
explanation: Convexity increases when a bond's cash flows are more spread out in time, so for a given duration, a coupon bond whose payments are dispersed across many dates has higher convexity than a zero-coupon bond whose single payment is concentrated at maturity. Higher convexity is desirable because it means the price gains more when rates fall and loses less when rates rise than duration alone predicts — an asymmetry that pays off precisely when rates move a lot. In a volatile environment large rate swings are likely, so the second-order convexity term becomes material and investors will pay up (accept lower yield) for the more convex bond.

prompt: What's the duration of a 5-year zero coupon bond? What are the annual payments received by the owner of a 5-year zero coupon bond?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state that a zero pays no interim coupons (single payment at maturity) and that duration equals maturity, i.e., 5 years.
explanation: Duration measures the weighted-average time until you receive a bond's cash flows, where each time is weighted by the present value of the cash flow arriving then. A zero coupon bond has only one cash flow — the full face value at maturity — so there is nothing to average against. With a single dated cash flow, the weighted average collapses to that single date, making duration exactly equal to maturity, which is 5 years here. The owner receives no annual payments at all; the return is earned entirely through buying the bond at a discount and collecting par at maturity.

prompt: Between a 5-year zero coupon bond and a 5-year bond with a 6% annual coupon, which has the higher duration and why? What does that imply about their relative price sensitivity to interest rate changes?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Must identify the zero as having higher duration (equal to maturity) because the coupon bond returns cash earlier, and connect higher duration to greater price sensitivity to rate moves.
explanation: The coupon bond delivers cash flows along the way, pulling the weighted-average timing forward and giving it a duration below 5 years. The zero returns everything only at maturity, so its duration is the full 5 years — the maximum possible for that term. Because duration measures price sensitivity to interest rates, the zero's price will move more for a given change in yield, making it the more volatile of the two. This is why zeros are prized (or feared) for their leverage to rate movements.

prompt: What is the relationship between a bond's price and its yield?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state prices and yields move inversely and give the intuition (fixed cash flows discounted at a changing rate).
explanation: A bond's cash flows are fixed at issuance, so the only way the market adjusts a bond to reflect a new required return is by changing its price. When required yields rise, each fixed future payment is worth less today, so the price falls; when yields fall, those same payments become more valuable and the price rises. That is why price and yield always move in opposite directions. Current yield (annual coupon divided by market price) captures part of this but ignores principal gain or loss, which is why yield-to-maturity is the fuller measure.

prompt: Two bonds have identical yields to maturity but very different price sensitivities to a 1% rise in rates. What characteristics would explain that difference?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should reference duration/maturity and coupon size as the drivers of differing price sensitivity despite equal yields.
explanation: Yield tells you the required return but says nothing about the timing of cash flows, which is what drives sensitivity. A longer-maturity bond, or one with a lower coupon, returns cash later and therefore has a higher duration, so its price falls more when rates rise. Two bonds can price to the same yield yet differ sharply in maturity and coupon structure, producing very different reactions to the same rate move. The distinguishing factor is duration, not yield.

prompt: Let's say that I have a bond with a 6 percent coupon. What happens to the market price as interest rates rise? How are the coupons affected?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state coupons are fixed/contractual and unaffected, while market price falls as rates rise, with the arbitrage/reallocation intuition.
explanation: The coupon is a contractual obligation set as a percentage of face value, so it never changes with market conditions — a 6% coupon pays 6% of par regardless of where rates go. What adjusts is the price. As market rates rise, investors can get a better return elsewhere for the same risk, so they sell this bond, pushing its price down until its effective yield matches the new market level. In short, the payment stream is frozen and the price does all the work to keep the bond competitive.

prompt: If rates rise sharply right after you buy that 6% bond at par, are you necessarily worse off if you hold it to maturity rather than sell? Explain.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should distinguish mark-to-market loss from realized outcome, and address reinvestment of coupons at higher rates.
explanation: If you hold to maturity, you still collect every 6% coupon and full par at the end, so your originally locked-in yield is realized regardless of interim price swings — you only crystallize a loss if you sell. However, there is an opportunity cost: you are stuck earning 6% while the market now offers more, and you can reinvest your coupons at those higher rates. So you are not worse off in nominal terms on this bond, but you are worse off relative to what you could have earned had you waited. The distinction is between mark-to-market pain and realized return.

prompt: Why do bonds trade at a discount / premium?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must explain that a fixed coupon no longer matches the market's required return (due to rate or credit changes), so price adjusts to a discount or premium to normalize the effective yield.
explanation: A bond is issued at par with a coupon set to match what the market demands at that moment for that credit. Over time, market rates move and the issuer's credit quality changes, but the coupon is locked, so it stops reflecting the true cost of capital lenders now require. The price then adjusts — down to a discount if the fixed coupon is now too stingy, up to a premium if it is now generous — so that a new buyer earns exactly the risk-adjusted return the market currently demands. Price is the market's lever for reconciling a fixed coupon with a moving required yield.

prompt: A bond's coupon is unchanged but it moves from trading at a premium to trading at a discount over six months. List the possible causes and explain the mechanism for each.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should cite rising benchmark rates and/or credit deterioration, explaining that both raise the required yield above the fixed coupon.
explanation: Two forces can do this. First, benchmark interest rates could have risen, so the market now demands more than the fixed coupon offers, pushing price below par. Second, the issuer's credit could have deteriorated, raising the risk premium investors require and again lifting the required yield above the coupon. In both cases the coupon is frozen while the required return climbs, so the price must fall to a discount to compensate a new buyer. Often it is a combination of both a rate move and a credit move.

prompt: What is an original issuance discount? Why might a company sell bonds with an OID?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must define OID as issuance below par and explain it delivers lender return at maturity rather than via coupons, plus at least one reason (rates rose between pricing and issuance, or deliberately low/zero coupon).
explanation: An original issue discount arises when a bond is sold for less than its face value at issuance, so part of the lender's compensation comes as the gap between the discounted purchase price and par repaid at maturity. A small OID often happens mechanically when market rates drift up between the time the coupon is fixed and the bond actually prints — the discount nudges the effective yield back up to market. More deliberately, a company may want to conserve cash by paying a lower coupon (or none at all, as with zeros), shifting the lender's return to a lump-sum principal gain at maturity. Accounting-wise the OID is amortized as non-cash interest expense over the bond's life.

prompt: How does OID affect an issuer's reported interest expense and cash flow differently from a normal cash-pay coupon, and why do PE sponsors sometimes favor such structures?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should explain OID accretes as non-cash interest expense reducing net income but not cash, and that sponsors value the cash preservation in leveraged deals.
explanation: With a cash-pay coupon, interest expense hits both the income statement and cash. With OID, the discount is accreted over the bond's life as interest expense that reduces reported earnings but consumes no cash until maturity, when the full par is repaid. This creates a tax shield and an expense on paper while preserving liquidity in the interim. PE sponsors like this in highly leveraged deals because it lets a stressed or growth-hungry portfolio company retain cash for operations and deleveraging, pushing the payment burden to a later refinancing or exit.

prompt: Given a coupon rate and YTM, how do you know if a bond is trading at a discount? At a premium? At par?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must give the rule: YTM > coupon = discount, YTM < coupon = premium, YTM = coupon = par, with the reasoning that YTM captures both coupon and principal gain/loss.
explanation: The coupon rate only tells you the income return; YTM tells you the total return including whatever principal gain or loss you get by holding to maturity. If YTM exceeds the coupon, the extra return must be coming from price appreciation toward par, which means you bought below par — a discount. If YTM is below the coupon, you must be losing some principal as the price declines toward par, which means you paid above par — a premium. When YTM equals the coupon there is no principal movement, so the bond trades at par.

prompt: A bond trades at a premium and is callable at par in two years. Why might its yield-to-call be materially lower than its yield-to-maturity, and why does that matter to an investor?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should explain that a premium bond loses principal down to call price sooner if called, compressing return, so YTC < YTM and investors should price to the worst case (yield-to-worst).
explanation: When a premium bond is bought above par but is callable at par, an early call forces the price loss to happen sooner, over a shorter horizon, which drags the realized yield below the yield-to-maturity. Because the issuer will call precisely when it is advantageous to them (rates fell), the investor should assume the worst outcome. This is why practitioners compute yield-to-worst — the lower of yield-to-call and yield-to-maturity — and price the bond accordingly. Ignoring the call would overstate the return an investor can actually rely on.

prompt: What are different risks associated with debt?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Should identify at least interest rate, prepayment/reinvestment, and default/credit risk, with a sentence on what drives each.
explanation: Debt investors face several distinct risks that all boil down to either the price of money changing or the borrower failing to pay. Interest rate risk means that when market rates rise, existing fixed-coupon debt becomes less attractive so its price falls to make the yield competitive. Prepayment and reinvestment risk are two sides of a falling-rate world: borrowers refinance to cheaper debt, so lenders lose their high-yielding asset and must redeploy the returned cash at now-lower rates. Default (credit) risk is the chance the borrower can't meet interest or principal, and it is cushioned when the company holds hard assets that provide recovery value relative to the size of the debt. Good answers tie each risk to the direction of rates or the health of the borrower.

prompt: You hold a bond with high duration in an environment where you expect the central bank to cut rates aggressively. Which risks help you and which hurt you, and how would a call feature change your view?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should note falling rates raise bond prices (helps) but introduce prepayment/reinvestment risk, and a call feature caps the upside since the issuer will redeem when it's advantageous to them.
explanation: Falling rates are generally good for a fixed-rate bondholder because the price rises as the coupon looks increasingly attractive versus new issuance, and long duration amplifies that gain. However, the same rate cuts trigger prepayment risk: the issuer wants to refinance at lower rates, and a call feature lets them do exactly that, redeeming your high-coupon bond and forcing you to reinvest at lower prevailing rates. So a call option asymmetrically favors the issuer and truncates your price upside, which is why callable bonds trade cheaper and why yield-to-worst becomes the relevant metric.

prompt: You have a 10% PIK bond with a 3 year maturity. What price must you buy it at for a 15% IRR?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must compound the PIK to ~133 over 3 years, convert 15% IRR over 3 years to ~1.5x MOIC, and divide to get an entry price of ~85-90.
explanation: A PIK (payment-in-kind) bond pays no cash; instead the coupon accrues onto the principal, so a 10% PIK on 100 grows to 110, 121, and ~133 by year three. To earn a 15% IRR over three years you need your money to multiply by roughly 1.15 cubed, which is about 1.5x (a handy shortcut: 15% for 3 years ≈ 1.5x MOIC). Since you receive 133 at exit and want that to represent 1.5x your entry, you divide 133 by 1.5 to get an entry price of roughly 88. So you'd need to buy the bond at about 85-90 to hit the target return.

prompt: Same 10% PIK bond, 3-year maturity, but now you can buy it at 70. What approximate IRR do you earn, and how does that compare to a cash-pay bond bought at 70?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should compute MOIC = 133/70 ≈ 1.9x over 3 years implying ~24% IRR, and note the cash-pay version returns coupons earlier so its IRR is higher for the same MOIC due to earlier cash flow timing.
explanation: The PIK grows to ~133 and buying at 70 gives a MOIC of about 1.9x over three years, which corresponds to roughly a 24% IRR (1.9^(1/3) ≈ 1.24). The key subtlety is timing: a PIK returns all value at maturity, whereas a cash-pay bond hands you coupons each year that you can reinvest, so for the same total dollars returned the cash-pay bond delivers a higher IRR because money arrives sooner. This is why distressed and mezzanine investors watch the cash-vs-PIK split carefully — it materially affects realized returns even at identical prices.

prompt: A distressed bond has a current yield of 11% and trades at 80 with maturity in 5 years. Assuming the bond is money-good (i.e., the full principal amount is repaid), what's the IRR on the investment?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Should combine current yield (~11%) with the annualized pull-to-par appreciation (~5%/yr from 80 to 100 over 5 years) for a total IRR of roughly 16%.
explanation: A bond's total return to a holder has two pieces: the income you collect (the coupon relative to price) and the capital gain or loss as the price moves toward par at maturity. Here the current yield of 11% captures the coupon income on your 80 purchase price. Buying at 80 and getting repaid 100 is a 25% gain spread over 5 years, which is roughly 5% per year of price appreciation as the bond pulls to par. Adding the ~11% income and ~5% appreciation gives an approximate IRR of ~16%; this is a quick mental estimate, and the true YTM would be slightly different due to compounding but close enough for an interview.

prompt: Why is the simple 'current yield plus annualized price appreciation' shortcut only an approximation of true yield to maturity, and would it overstate or understate the real YTM for a discount bond?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should explain the shortcut ignores compounding and the reinvestment of coupons plus the timing of the price gain, and note it typically slightly understates true YTM for a deep-discount bond because the effective return on invested capital is higher.
explanation: The shortcut treats income and price appreciation as simple linear add-ons, but true YTM is the single discount rate that equates the present value of all cash flows to the price, which accounts for compounding and the exact timing of each coupon and the final principal repayment. Because coupons are received and implicitly reinvested along the way, and because the current yield uses the discounted purchase price as its base, the linear approximation doesn't perfectly capture the internal rate. For a discount bond the coupon is earned on a base of 80 rather than 100, and the gain compounds, so the crude method tends to slightly understate the real YTM, though for interviews the approximation is directionally reliable.

prompt: A sponsor-owned company's EBITDA drops to $50mm in FY2. At entry, the company had 3 turns of first lien debt (@ 5% coupon) and 2 turns of second lien debt (@ 10% coupon). The second lien debt is trading at 80. What information would you need in order to determine whether or not you should invest in the second lien tranche of debt?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must identify that you need current EV (via entry multiple applied to current EBITDA) and the amount of first lien debt ahead of the second lien, to assess whether EV covers the second lien in a downside/recovery scenario.
explanation: Deciding whether to buy a tranche of debt at a discount is fundamentally about whether the enterprise value covers your claim after everything senior to you is paid. The second lien sits behind the first lien, so you need to know how much first lien debt is ahead of you and what the whole business is worth today. You can estimate current EV by applying the sponsor's entry multiple to the current $50mm EBITDA (holding the multiple constant), and estimate the first lien balance as 3 turns of the entry EBITDA assuming no paydown. If EV comfortably exceeds first lien plus your second lien claim, the debt at 80 is likely cheap; if EV barely covers or falls short of the first lien, the second lien is impaired and 80 may be too rich. The core skill is building a recovery waterfall.

prompt: Suppose the entry multiple was 8x on $75mm of entry EBITDA, and EBITDA has fallen to $50mm with the multiple holding. First lien is 3 turns and second lien is 2 turns of entry EBITDA. Is the second lien at 80 attractive? Walk through the recovery math.
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should compute entry EV metrics, current EV = 8x*50 = 400, first lien = 3*75 = 225, second lien = 2*75 = 150; second lien covered since 400-225=175 > 150, implying full recovery so 80 is cheap.
explanation: Build the waterfall: current EV is the multiple times current EBITDA, 8x times $50mm equals $400mm. First lien is 3 turns of the $75mm entry EBITDA, or $225mm, and it gets paid first, leaving $175mm of value. The second lien claim is 2 turns of entry EBITDA, or $150mm, and since $175mm of residual value exceeds that $150mm claim, the second lien is fully money-good and should trade near par, not 80. Buying it at 80 for a fully covered claim implies meaningful upside as it pulls back to par plus coupon, so it looks attractive — the key caveat being your assumption that the entry multiple still holds and EBITDA doesn't deteriorate further.

prompt: What is the difference between Yield to Maturity and Yield to Worst?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must define YTM as the return if held to maturity and YTW as the lower of YTM and yield-to-call across all call dates, noting call premiums can partly offset lost coupons.
explanation: Yield to maturity is the IRR you earn assuming you hold the bond all the way to its stated maturity, collecting every coupon and the final principal. Many bonds, however, are callable, meaning the issuer can redeem them early on specified dates, which cuts short your coupon stream and changes your return — that scenario's IRR is the yield to call. Yield to worst is simply the most conservative outcome: the lowest yield across the maturity scenario and every possible call date, giving the investor the worst-case return the issuer could impose. Call protection (a premium the issuer pays to call early) can lift the yield-to-call by handing you a bit extra, but YTW still assumes the issuer acts in its own interest.

prompt: Under what conditions would an issuer choose to call a bond, and why does that timing make yield-to-call the binding constraint in yield-to-worst for a premium bond?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should explain issuers call when they can refinance cheaper (rates fell or credit improved), which happens precisely when the bond trades at a premium, making the early redemption scenario the worst outcome for the investor.
explanation: An issuer calls a bond when it can replace that debt more cheaply, typically because market rates have fallen or its own credit has improved, so it retires the high-coupon bond and refinances at a lower rate. That is exactly the situation in which the bond trades above par (a premium), since a high coupon in a low-rate world is what pushes the price up. From the investor's perspective, being called strips away the remaining premium and future above-market coupons, so the yield-to-call is lower than yield-to-maturity and therefore becomes the worst case that defines YTW. The issuer's incentive to call and the investor's downside are two sides of the same coin.

prompt: Following on from "What is the difference between Yield to Maturity and Yield to Worst?" — What can you say about YTW and premium / discount bonds generally?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
guidance: Must state that for premium bonds YTW equals yield-to-call (YTC < YTM) and for discount bonds YTW equals YTM (YTM < YTC).
explanation: The relationship follows directly from when an issuer would rationally call. A premium bond carries an above-market coupon, so the issuer wants to call it early to stop overpaying; early redemption shortens the high-coupon stream and gives a lower return, so yield-to-call sits below yield-to-maturity and YTW equals YTC. A discount bond has a below-market coupon, so the issuer has no reason to call — refinancing would mean giving up cheap debt — and holding it to maturity captures the full pull-to-par gain, so yield-to-maturity is the lower (binding worst-case) figure and YTW equals YTM. The unifying idea is that YTW always assumes the issuer does whatever is worst for you, which lines up with what is best for them.

prompt: A bond trades exactly at par with a coupon equal to prevailing market yield. What is the relationship between YTM, YTC, and YTW, and how sensitive is that to a small move in rates?
source_ref: Extends: Priced In — Debt Refresher
guidance: Should note at par YTM ≈ YTC ≈ coupon so YTW is roughly equal to all three, but a small rate drop pushes it to a premium (YTW=YTC) and a rise pushes it to a discount (YTW=YTM), so it's the knife-edge case.
explanation: When a bond trades at par with its coupon matching the market yield, there is no premium or discount to gain or lose, so yield to maturity and yield to call both approximately equal the coupon, and yield to worst sits right at that same level. This is the tipping point: if rates fall even slightly, the bond becomes a premium bond and the issuer's incentive to call kicks in, so YTW snaps to yield-to-call; if rates rise slightly, it becomes a discount bond with no call incentive, so YTW becomes yield-to-maturity. The par bond is therefore the knife-edge case where a tiny rate move determines which scenario binds.

prompt: You have a company with $500 million of senior debt and $500 million of junior debt. The senior debt has an interest rate of L+500 and, in default, would recover 70 percent; the junior debt would recover 30 percent in default. What should the interest rate be on the junior debt?
source_ref: Priced In — Debt Refresher / Loose Ends
